(Agaricus campestris) – pieczarka polna,: (Agaricus campestris) – Polish folk names: 'pieczarka polna', 'polowa', 'ogrodowa', 'piekarka'. From May to November in meadows, pastures, fields, field boundaries, gardens and ditches – places rich in nitrogen compounds. Cap spherical, then convex and finally spread out, whitish. Stem short, thick and solid, with a ring at the top. Edible. Confused with poisonous white amanitas ('muchomor' (Polish name)), e.g. the venomous one. Unlike them it has no bulb or volva at the stem base and no whitish gills; in champignons the gills are pink, reddish-brown, up to brown-black.
(Agaricus xanthoderma) – pieczarka cuchn: (Agaricus xanthoderma) – Polish folk names: 'pieczarka cuchnaca', 'karbolowa'. From May to October in deciduous forests, parks, on roadsides and among grasses, in fertile places rich in nitrogen. Often grows in fairy rings. Cap semicircular, convex, sometimes spread out, whitish, cream or grey-brown. Gills pinkish-grey. Stem whitish with a thin and delicate ring, bulbously widened at the base. Flesh white, turning chrome yellow when cut at the stem base. Smell unpleasant, of carbolic acid (especially when boiling or frying). Poisonous!
(Amanita pantherina) Od lipca do paździe: (Amanita pantherina) From July to October in coniferous and deciduous forests, on dry and sandy soils, under pines, spruces, oaks and beeches. Cap hemispherical, then convex, and finally spread out, with a striate margin, brownish with white spots that rain may wash off. Stem cylindrical, slender, smooth, with a hanging smooth ring and a volva in the form of rolls, on a bulbous base. Smell of radish. Strongly poisonous! Sometimes confused with 'czubajka kania' (Polish name).
(Amanita phalloides) – muchomor sromotni: (Amanita phalloides) – Polish folk names: 'muchomor sromotnikowy'. From July to October in deciduous and mixed forests, singly or in groups. Cap convex, then flat, greenish (sometimes white), shiny. Stem with a zigzag pattern, with a hanging ring, cylindrical with a bulbously thickened base and a white, sac-like, torn volva. Smell bland, sweetish. Deadly poisonous! Confused with 'gaska zielonka' (Polish name), 'golabek zielonawy' (Polish name) and champignons.
(Amanita porphyria) Od lipca do paździer: (Amanita porphyria) From July to October, usually in groups in thinned pine forests, on sandy and acid soils, mainly under pines, birches and spruces (often among bilberry). Cap convex, then spread out, brownish-grey to grey-violet, with a smooth or slightly striate margin, dry, covered with irregular grey-violet patches. Gills white and crowded. Stem whitish or grey, later with a violet tinge, cylindrical and slender, solid, later hollow, with a thickened bulbous base, with a ring. Flesh white, violet under the cap skin, with a taste of radish and a smell of musty potatoes. Inedible, weakly poisonous! Confused with 'gaska nieksztaltna' (Polish name) and 'muchomor czerwonawy' (Polish name).
(Amanita verna) Od czerwca do październi: (Amanita verna) From June to October, quite rarely in lowland deciduous and mixed forests on calcareous soils. Prefers warm sites. Cap bell-shaped, then convex, white or cream, smooth with a striate margin. Gills white, rounded at the cap margin. Stem slender, cylindrical, white and smooth with a bulbous base surrounded by a white, spreading and torn volva. Ring white, thin and not very large. Flesh white, brittle. Deadly poisonous! Confused with young champignons and 'majowka wiosenna' (Polish name).
(Amanita virosa) Od lipca do październik: (Amanita virosa) From July to October, mainly on poor, moist and acid soils, in coniferous forests, less often in deciduous ones, under spruces, pines, birches, oaks and beeches. Cap bell-shaped, then flatter, whitish with a striate margin. Stem cylindrical, scaly-fibrous with a bulbously thickened base and a membranous volva; ring vestigial or absent. Smell of radish. Deadly poisonous! Young fruiting bodies are confused with champignons.
(Armillaria ostoyae) – podpieńka, pniokó: (Armillaria ostoyae) – Polish folk names: 'podpienka', 'pniokowka'. From September to November in dense clusters on coniferous and deciduous trees and on stumps. Cap hemispherical, then spread out, even depressed, beige or brown with small, dark scales. Stem cylindrical and curved with a thickened base, yellowish-brown, bast-fibrous with a distinct ring. Produces black mycelial cords (rhizomorphs). Only the caps are edible. Undercooked it may be harmful. Confused with 'maslanka wiazkowa' (Polish name) ('lysiczka trujaca' (Polish name)).
(Boletus edulis) – prawdziwek, grzyb bia: (Boletus edulis) – Polish folk names: 'prawdziwek', 'grzyb bialy'. From June to November in coniferous forests, less often in deciduous and mixed forests, under spruces, pines and birches. Most abundant in mountain spruce stands. Cap semicircular, then convex, matt, from white to various shades of brown. The underside of the cap is made of tubes whose openings (pores) are at first whitish, cream, later yellow-green, and do not change colour when touched. Stem solid, barrel-shaped, later club-shaped, whitish, light brown with a fine net of veins, white and felty at the base. Edible. Confused with 'goryczak zolciowy' (Polish name) and 'borowik szatanski' (Polish name).
(Boletus calopus) – borowik grubotrzonow: (Boletus calopus) – Polish folk names: 'borowik grubotrzonowy'. From June to October, mainly in foothill and mountain forests of southern Poland and in Pomerania, under spruces and beeches, on acid soils. Cap semicircular, then convex with irregularly bent margins, grey-brown with a yellowish tinge, smooth, matt and dry, suede-like. Underside lemon yellow, yellow-olive, turns blue when touched. Stem thick, strong, solid and club-shaped, yellow at the top, red in the middle and brown-red at the bottom, with a distinct net everywhere. Flesh hard, firm, yellowish, pink at the bottom of the stem. Turns blue when cut. Taste at first mild, then bitter. Poisonous! Confused with 'borowik ceglastopory' (Polish name).
(Calocybe gambosa) – majówka wiosenna, g: (Calocybe gambosa) – Polish folk names: 'majowka wiosenna', 'gaska majowa'. From April to June singly, sometimes in groups (in fairy rings) in meadows, pastures, forest edges, forest clearings, parks and thickets. Cap bell-shaped with an inrolled margin, then flattened, cream with a yellowish tinge, smooth and dry. Gills whitish to cream, crowded and thin, narrow, notched at the stem. Stem of equal thickness or club-shaped, solid or spongy, whitish. Flesh firm, whitish, with a mealy taste and smell. Edible. Confused with 'wieruszka zatokowata' (Polish name), 'strzepiak ceglasty' (Polish name) and white amanitas ('muchomor' (Polish name)).
(Cantharellus cibarius) – kurka, lisica,: (Cantharellus cibarius) – Polish folk names: 'kurka', 'lisica', 'liszka'. From June to November in coniferous (pine, spruce) and deciduous (oak, beech) forests, in dense groups in moss or fallen leaves. Fruiting body convex, then funnel-shaped with an irregular margin, yellow. Stem of the same colour, widened at the top, solid. Ridge-like gills run down the stem. The taste of the raw fruiting body is acrid, peppery. Confused with the inedible 'lisowka pomaranczowa' (Polish name), the so-called false chanterelle.
(Rozites caperatus) – niemka, turek, byd: (Rozites caperatus) – Polish folk names: 'niemka', 'turek', 'bydlarka', 'chocholka', 'lesna pieczarka', 'szampion'. From July to October in groups in coniferous forests, mainly pine and spruce, often among bilberry and heather. Cap egg-shaped, then convex and flattened with a small hump, whitish, yellowish or greyish-yellow, sometimes with a pale blue tinge, cracked at the margins. Gills yellowish, then brown, crowded, with a notched edge. Stem white, yellowish, cylindrical, thickened at the base, longitudinally striate, solid, with a narrow membranous ring that disappears with time. Flesh whitish, fleshy, yellowish under the cap skin, with a pleasant smell and taste. Edible. Confused with 'strzepiak ceglasty' (Polish name).
(Entoloma sinuatum) – dzwonkówka trująca: (Entoloma sinuatum) – Polish folk names: 'dzwonkowka trujaca'. From June to September singly or in groups in open deciduous forests, forest clearings, under oaks, beeches and hornbeams, on clay and calcareous soils. Prefers warm and moist sites. Cap semicircular with inrolled margins, then convex and finally flat, smooth with an easily peeling skin, whitish, cream to grey-brown. Gills whitish, then pinkish, sinuately notched at the stem. Stem whitish or light yellow, cylindrical or slightly club-shaped, solid, later spongy and hollow, without a ring. Flesh white, shiny, with a floury taste and smell. Strongly poisonous! Confused with 'gesnica' (Polish name) ('majowka' (Polish name)) 'wiosenna' (Polish name) and champignons.
(Galerina marginata) – hełmówka jadowita: (Galerina marginata) – Polish folk names: 'helmowka jadowita'. From June to October, singly or in groups on decaying coniferous wood, less often deciduous. Cap semicircular, convex, then flat, with a depression or hump in the centre and an even sharp margin, in various shades of brown (darker when wet). When young, with fibrils of the veil at the margin. Gills yellowish, light brown, then red-brown, broad and attached to the stem. Stem in various shades of brown, cylindrical, solid, then hollow with a skin-like, short-lived, whitish or brown ring, below which it is whitish-fibrillose. Flesh brownish, thin, with a floury taste and smell. Deadly poisonous! Confused with 'luszczak zmienny' (Polish name).
(Gyromitra esculenta) Od marca do maja w: (Gyromitra esculenta) From March to May in pine and spruce stands on dry and sandy soils, in clear-cuts, usually directly on bare soil. Head irregularly spherical and folded, hollow inside, chestnut or dark brown. Stem short, cylindrical, whitish. Flesh brittle and waxy. Pleasant smell. Deadly poisonous! Confused with 'smardz' (Polish name).
(Hygrophoropsis auriantiaca) – fałszywa: (Hygrophoropsis auriantiaca) – Polish folk names: 'falszywa kurka', 'jadowita kurka', 'pieprznik pomaranczowy'. From September to November in coniferous and mixed forests. Cap convex, then funnel-shaped with inrolled margins, orange or brownish, matt, elastic. Gills intensely orange. Stem thin, slender, widened upwards, smooth. Inedible! Confused with 'pieprznik jadalny' (Polish name), that is the chanterelle ('kurka' (Polish name)).
(Hypholoma fasciculare) – łysiczka trują: (Hypholoma fasciculare) – Polish folk names: 'lysiczka trujaca', 'maslanka trujaca', 'opienka trujaca', 'opienka falszywa'. From May to December, commonly in clusters on stumps of coniferous and deciduous trees. Cap hemispherical, then convex and finally flat with a hump, yellow or rusty brown, with a darker centre, smooth and shiny. Stem cylindrical, slender, bent and hollow, covered with fibres. Flesh with an unpleasant smell. The whole bunch is fused at the base. Poisonous! Confused with honey fungi ('opienki' (Polish name)).
(Inocybe erubescens) Od czerwca do wrześ: (Inocybe erubescens) From June to September (very rarely in late autumn) in thinned deciduous forests, thickets, old parks, under oaks, beeches, hornbeams and lindens. Cap bell-shaped with an inrolled margin, then flat with a hump, radially cracked with turned-up margins, whitish, yellowish, even brick-brown. Gills whitish, then brownish, crowded, turning red when damaged. Stem white, then brick-coloured, cylindrical, solid, bent and thickened at the base, dry and fibrous. Flesh fleshy, turning red when cut, with a sweetish, fruity smell and a mild taste. Deadly poisonous (contains a lot of muscarine)! Confused with 'plachetka zwyczajna' (Polish name) and 'gesnica (majowka) wiosenna' (Polish name).
(Kuehneromyces mutabilis) – łuskwiak Od: (Kuehneromyces mutabilis) – Polish folk names: 'luskwiak'. From May to November in forests, parks and tree stands, on wood, stumps and fallen trunks, in dense bundles. Prefers the wood of deciduous trees, less often coniferous. Cap semicircular, then flat with a hump, from yellow to rusty brown, smooth with a darker striate margin. Gills of a similar changeable colour. Stem cylindrical, hollow, bast-like, rusty brown, darker at the base, slender and thin. The stem below the disappearing ring is covered with brown scales. Flesh in the cap whitish and soft, in the stem hard, rusty brown. Edible (woody stems should be cut off). Confused with the poisonous 'helmowka obrzezona' (Polish name).
(Lactarius deliciosus) – rycek, rydzyk,: (Lactarius deliciosus) – Polish folk names: 'rycek', 'rydzyk', 'ryzyk'. From August to November singly or in groups under pines. Cap convex, then funnel-shaped, brick-orange with a touch of green, with concentric rings. Gills orange, turn green when crushed. Stem cylindrical with dark spots. Orange milk in the flesh. A mushroom that is becoming ever rarer. It is sometimes confused with the poisonous ones: 'mleczaj welnianka' (Polish name) and 'krowiak podwiniety' (Polish name).
(Lactarius torminosus) – bawełnianka, we: (Lactarius torminosus) – Polish folk names: 'bawelnianka', 'welniak', 'rydz konski', 'kosmaty'. From August to October in coniferous and mixed forests, exclusively under birches. Cap convex, then flat and funnel-shaped with an inrolled margin, orange to light brown with dark concentric rings, hairy. Stem cylindrical, short and massive, smooth. Exudes abundant white milk that tastes burning. Poisonous! Confused with 'rydz' (Polish name).
(Lycoperdon perlatum) – purchawka szorst: (Lycoperdon perlatum) – Polish folk names: 'purchawka szorstka', 'purchadka', 'kurzawka'. From June to November commonly in coniferous and deciduous forests, in meadows and pastures. Resembles an inverted plump bottle or a pear. The white fruiting body is covered with spines. Inside also white and compact, later it darkens and takes on a musty smell. Edible as long as its interior is white and elastic. It is sometimes confused with the poisonous 'tegoskor cytrynowy' (Polish name).
(Macrolepiota procera) – kania, sowa Od: (Macrolepiota procera) – Polish folk names: 'kania', 'sowa'. From July to November in deciduous and mixed forests, by roads, in clearings and clear-cuts, in grassy places. Grows in groups. Cap egg-shaped, then umbrella-shaped with a small hump at the top, dry, cracked, covered with spreading scales, in various shades of brown. Stem long, slender, bulbous at the base, in the upper part with a double, movable ring, hollow inside. Breaks off easily from the cap. Only the cap is edible. Sometimes confused with the spotted amanita ('muchomor plamisty' (Polish name)).
(Marasmius oreades) – podróżniczka, przy: (Marasmius oreades) – Polish folk names: 'podrozniczka', 'przydrozka', 'tancowka'. From May to October in pastures, meadows, grassy roadsides, outside forests. Very common, grows in rows or fairy rings. Cap semicircular, conical, then flat, with a darker hump, flesh-coloured, light brown, darker when wet, smooth. Gills of a similar colour, fairly thick and widely spaced. Stem cylindrical, fibrous and bast-like, with whitish mycelium at the base, smooth. Flesh whitish, elastic with an aromatic mushroom smell and a mild taste. Edible (only the caps are used). Confused with the poisonous 'lejkowka lisciowa' (Polish name).
(Morchella esculenta) – smardz zwyczajny: (Morchella esculenta) – Polish folk names: 'smardz zwyczajny', 'smorz'. From April to May, after spring rains, in thinned deciduous forests and parks, mainly under ashes, elms, maples and beeches. It consists of a spherical or egg-shaped head, hollow inside, and a squat stem widened at the base. On the cap, coloured from grey to brownish-yellow, there are characteristic folds and pits surrounded by ribs – like a honeycomb. Under partial species protection outside gardens, horticultural crops, forest nurseries and green areas. Confused with the poisonous 'piestrzenica kasztanowata' (Polish name).
(Boletus luridiformis) – gniewus, pociec: (Boletus luridiformis) – Polish folk names: 'gniewus', 'pociec', 'ceglak'. From May to October in coniferous and deciduous forests, on acid soils. Cap semicircular dark brown, then cushion-shaped with a brick or olive tinge, matt, suede-like, sticky in wet weather. Underside yellowish-olive, then brick-red, turns blue when pressed. Stem yellowish with red tufts or grains, without a net, red-brown at the base, cylindrical or slightly club-shaped, turning blue under pressure. Flesh yellow, turning blue when cut, with a mild taste and smell. Edible. Confused with the poisonous 'borowik grubotrzonowy' (Polish name).
(Paxillus involutus) – olszówka Od lipca: (Paxillus involutus) – Polish folk names: 'olszowka'. From July to October commonly in moist coniferous and deciduous forests, parks, often under birches and alders, and also pines, spruces and oaks. Cap convex, then flat and funnel-shaped with an inrolled margin, velvety, brown Stem short, cylindrical, stocky, narrowed at the base. Formerly considered edible. Poisonous! It is sometimes confused with 'mleczaj rudy' (Polish name) and with 'rydz' (Polish name) – unlike it, it does not exude milk.
(Russula emetica) – serojeszka mierzliwa: (Russula emetica) – Polish folk names: 'serojeszka mierzliwa', 'gorzkowka'. From June to November in fairly moist pine and spruce forests, on peat bogs. Cap convex, then flat and finally depressed, reddish, sticky during rain. Stem cylindrical, smooth and brittle, mostly pure white. Smell fruity. Confused with 'golabek wyborny' (Polish name) (edible). Unlike it, 'golabek wymiotny' (Polish name) has a sharp and burning taste.
(Russula vesca) – gołąbek jadalny, suroj: (Russula vesca) – Polish folk names: 'golabek jadalny', 'surojadka'. From June to October in deciduous, mixed and coniferous forests, especially under oaks, beeches, pines and spruces. Cap hemispherical, then convex or flat with a depression in the middle, reddish, flesh-pink, in places discoloured to an ochre colour. Skin sticky during rain, often does not reach the margin of the cap. Stem cylindrical, solid, whitish. One of the tastiest russulas. It is sometimes confused with the poisonous 'golabek wymiotny' (Polish name), which has a burning taste.
(Russula virescens) – surowiatka, suroja: (Russula virescens) – Polish folk names: 'surowiatka', 'surojadka zielonawa', 'siwek'. From June to October, most often under oaks, beeches and birches in deciduous and mixed forests. Cap spherical, then spread out with a depression in the middle, grey-green, green-blue or olive. Initially smooth, quickly cracked in a characteristic pattern of small blocks. Confused with the deadly poisonous 'muchomor zielonawy' (Polish name) ('sromotnikowy' (Polish name)).
(Scleroderma citrinum) – bycze jaja, fał: (Scleroderma citrinum) – Polish folk names: 'bycze jaja', 'falszywa trufla', 'trufel'. From June to November in dense groups in coniferous and deciduous forests. Prefers sunny places. Fruiting body spherical or tuberous, resembles a potato, yellowish or brown, without a stem, covered with protruding scales. The interior of the fruiting body is white and hard, then black, resembling ground poppy seed. Smell strong, spicy. Poisonous! It may be confused with 'purchawka chropowata' (Polish name).
(Tricholoma equestre) – zielonka, gąska: (Tricholoma equestre) – Polish folk names: 'zielonka', 'gaska zolta'. From September to November (sometimes in December) common in coniferous forests on sands. Singly or in groups, mainly under pine. Only the upper part of the cap protrudes from the moss or soil. Cap with a bent-in margin, then spread out, yellow-green to brown-olive, darker in the centre, smooth. Usually sandy, sticky during rain. Gills bright yellow, thin and brittle. Stem solid, cylindrical, thickened at the base, yellow-green. Flesh hard, fleshy, whitish, with a mild taste. Edible. However, it may cause dangerous poisoning if larger amounts are eaten regularly. Confused with 'gaska siarkowa' (Polish name) and even the death cap ('muchomor sromotnikowy' (Polish name)).
(Tricholoma portentosum) – gąska siwa, s: (Tricholoma portentosum) – Polish folk names: 'gaska siwa', 'siwka', 'siwuszka'. From September to December, in groups in coniferous forests on sandy soils. In similar places and at a similar time as 'gaska zielonka' (Polish name). Cap flat with a hump in the centre, greyish with a violet-brown tinge, smooth, with black radial fibres. Stem whitish, cylindrical, solid, in old age, like the gills, with a yellow-green sheen. Confused with poisonous amanitas ('muchomor' (Polish name)), e.g. the porfirowy one ('muchomor porfirowy' (Polish name)).
(Tricholoma sulphureum) Od sierpnia do l: (Tricholoma sulphureum) From August to November in deciduous and mixed forests (mainly on sands), under pines, oaks and beeches. Cap convex, with a hump, yellow-olive to brownish-yellow, dry and smooth, sometimes with fine fibrils. Gills yellow, rather distant and thick. Stem slender, cylindrical, yellow-olive with a brown tinge, dry with fibrils. Flesh sulphur-yellow, thin and fibrous, with an unpleasant taste and a suffocating smell of carbide. Inedible, weakly poisonous. Confused with 'gaska zielonka' (Polish name).
(Tylopilus felleus) – borowik żółciowy,: (Tylopilus felleus) – Polish folk names: 'borowik zolciowy', 'podgrzybek gorzki'. From June to October in coniferous and mixed forests, mainly under pines and spruces. Does not occur in the mountains. Cap semicircular, then convex or flat, light brown; suede-like in young ones, smooth in older ones, sticky during rain. Tubes and pores whitish, with age or when touched they change colour to pink to pink-brown. Stem solid, thickened at the bottom, lighter than the cap, with a distinct brownish net. Flesh white, very bitter, but with a pleasant smell. Inedible! Causes severe gastrointestinal disorders. Confused with 'borowik szlachetny' (Polish name).
Kapelusz borowika jest mięsisty, wypukły: The cap of the 'borowik' (Polish name) is fleshy, convex, dry and matt, in colour from sandy to chestnut. The tubes in young specimens are almost white, in older ones yellow-olive. Stem thick, barrel-shaped, sand-coloured with a whitish net of veins. The inedible 'goryczak zolciowy' (Polish name) is characterised by a stem with a brown net with long meshes and a pink-coloured tube layer. In young specimens the tubes are dirty white. Cap cushion-shaped, suede-like. Even a small addition of 'goryczak' (Polish name) to a dish prepared from 'borowiki' (Polish name) will make it unfit to eat because of the strong bitterness.
Cechą rozpoznawczą czubajki kani jest zy: The distinguishing features of the 'czubajka kania' (Polish name) are the zigzag pattern on the stem, the movable ring, the cap with a hump, the white, unchanging flesh, the bulbous base without a volva. A 'czubajka' (Polish name) that causes poisoning, such as the 'czubajka czerwieniejaca' (Polish name), can be told apart by the distinct, protruding scales on the cap, the red colouring of the gills and stem after damage, and the absence of a darker pattern on the stem. In turn, the poisonous 'czubajka ostroluskowa' (Polish name) has a cap covered with conical scales, a non-sliding ring and an unpleasant smell. A mistake between the 'czubajka kania' (Polish name) and the 'muchomor zielonawy' (Polish name) is a deadly danger. It has a greenish, smooth (without patches) cap without a hump, an immovable ring and a bulb with a volva. In turn, the 'muchomor plamisty' (Polish name) is distinguished from the 'kania' (Polish name) by lighter, white patches on a brown cap that has no hump, a hanging ring and a bulb at the base of the stem.
Czubajka kania, czubajka czerwieniejąca,: 'Czubajka kania' (Polish name), 'czubajka czerwieniejaca' (Polish name), 'ostroluskowa' (Polish name), and the deadly poisonous amanitas
Gąskę zielonkę możemy pomylić z gąską si: We may confuse the 'gaska zielonka' (Polish name) with the 'gaska siarkowa' (Polish name), which is poisonous when raw, and when cooked – inedible because of the unpleasant smell of carbide. Other characteristic features of the edible 'gaska' (Polish name) are yellow, densely arranged gills, a smell of flour and whitish flesh.
Łuszczak zmienny zmienia barwę w zależno: The 'luszczak zmienny' (Polish name) changes colour depending on the degree of moisture. When dry it is faded and lighter at the margin, when moist it becomes honey-brown and a little slimy. Gills from white, through cinnamon to red-brown. Stem hollow with a brown ring, scaly below it, bald in older ones. The 'luszczak zmienny' (Polish name) has a pleasant mushroom smell and grows on the wood of deciduous trees. We may confuse it with the deadly poisonous 'helmowka jadowita' (Polish name), which gives off a smell of flour, grows on the wood of coniferous trees, and has a white ring below which the stem has a structure with white fibrils.
Łuszczak zmienny, a śmiertelnie trująca: 'Luszczak zmienny' (Polish name) and the deadly poisonous 'helmowka jadowita' (Polish name)
Mleczaj rydz ma pomarańczowe blaszki, kt: The 'mleczaj rydz' (Polish name) has orange gills that turn green when damaged but never turn wine-red. The milk is carrot-coloured; as it dries it fades and turns grey-green, but never discolours to wine-red. It is also worth remembering that the 'mleczaj rydz' (Polish name) grows only under pines. A particular health hazard is a mistake with the 'mleczaj welnianka' (Polish name). Its gills are white, the milk burning and white. The fringed-tufted margin of the cap is characteristic. It grows only under birches. The toxic 'krowiak podwiniety' (Polish name), called 'olszowka' (Polish name), should also be avoided. This mushroom does not exude milk when damaged. Instead, the gills and stem turn red-brown.
Mleczaj rydz, a trujący mleczaj wełniank: 'Mleczaj rydz' (Polish name) and the poisonous 'mleczaj welnianka' (Polish name) and 'krowiak podwiniety' (Polish name)
Muchomor zielonawy jest jednym z najsiln: The 'muchomor zielonawy' (Polish name) is one of the most strongly poisonous mushrooms. The characteristic features of this mushroom are: always white, cream gills; a smooth cap surface; a hanging, non-sliding ring on the stem, under the cap; a thick bulb surrounded by a volva; a sweet smell resembling artificial honey. The edible species with which we may confuse it are the 'czubajka kania' (Polish name), the 'golabek zielonawy' (Polish name) and the 'gaska zielonka' (Polish name), that is mushrooms that also have gills. And this is the only feature they have in common. The 'czubajka kania' (Polish name) is distinguished by scales on the cap, a movable ring and a bulb without a volva. If during mushroom picking we are guided solely by the colour of the cap, a mistake may concern the 'golabek zielonawy' (Polish name). However, the 'golabek' (Polish name) has neither a ring nor a volva, the stem is smooth, and the surface of the cap in adult specimens is characteristically cracked into patches. When collecting young specimens, the poisonous amanita may also be confused with the 'gaska zielonka' (Polish name). Here the characteristic features distinguishing the 'gaska' (Polish name) are yellow gills, no ring and no volva, and a decidedly smaller size of adult specimens. In the case of mistaking edible mushrooms for the 'muchomor zielonawy' (Polish name) we must especially follow the rule of collecting only adult fruiting bodies that have already developed their characteristic features.
Śmiertelnie trujący muchomor zielonawy,: The deadly poisonous 'muchomor zielonawy' (Polish name) and similar edible species
Opieńka miodowa jest jadalnym grzybem, j: The 'opienka miodowa' (Polish name) is an edible mushroom, but only young caps are fit for consumption. We may confuse the 'opienka miodowa' (Polish name) with the 'maslanka wiazkowa' (Polish name). Both grow in dense groups on stumps, but the 'maslanka' (Polish name) is decidedly distinguished by a smooth cap, no ring and a very bitter taste.
Do pomyłki może dojść przy ocenie młodyc: A mistake may occur when assessing young fruiting bodies. Therefore let us remember to collect champignons when they have developed their distinguishing features. The most important feature is the gills of champignons. The edible ones are at first pale grey, then pink, and finally blackish. The poisonous 'pieczarka karbolowa' (Polish name) greatly resembles the edible champignon. In this case the 'pieczarka karbolowa' (Polish name) is decidedly distinguished by its smell and its reaction to damage. If it turns yellow after damage and at the same time smells unpleasant, we are dealing with the 'pieczarka karbolowa' (Polish name). If we want to make additionally sure, we can cut the champignon and place it in a bowl of hot water – the smell of carbolic acid will be more intense. The characteristic feature that distinguishes the 'muchomor jadowity' (Polish name) from edible champignons is the invariably white, or possibly slightly cream, gills throughout the life of this mushroom.
Pieczarki jadalne, pieczarka trująca (ka: Edible champignons, the poisonous (carbolic) 'pieczarka' (Polish name), and the deadly poisonous amanitas
Pieprznika jadalnego możemy pomylić z li: We may confuse the 'pieprznik jadalny' (Polish name) with the 'lisowka pomaranczowa' (Polish name). The false chanterelle will have the cap, gills and stem in the same orange colour. Elastic, soft and orange flesh. Stem decidedly narrower than that of the edible chanterelle and mostly of equal thickness or gently narrowing downwards. The 'pieprznik jadalny' (Polish name) can be recognised by the stem slightly lighter than the cap and the white flesh.
Smardz pojawia się w lasach już w kwietn: The 'smardz' (Polish name) appears in forests as early as April. It is distinguished by a fruiting body that is almost round or slightly elongated with wide pits. It is hollow throughout the cross-section. In turn, the 'piestrzenica kasztanowata' (Polish name) has an irregularly folded surface resembling a brain, and its cap is fused with the stem.
